newsitem.title: USA: Kmart shares rise sharply on takeover rumors.
newsitem.headline: Kmart shares rise sharply on takeover rumors.

text.p: Kmart Corp. stock, which hit a slump recently due to lagging discount store sales, rose sharply Tuesday on market rumors it is the target of a takeover by buyout firm Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co.

Troy, Mich.,-based Kmart, the nation's second-largest retailer, called the speculation a rumor and would not react to activity in its stock, which was the most heavily traded on the New York Stock Exchange.
"It's just a rumor," said Kmart spokeswoman Shawn Kahle. "We're not going to comment on it."
New York-based KKR also declined to comment.
Still, Wall Street analysts noted KKR has recently raised a large fund and said a deal was not out of the question.
"You never say never, but I'm not putting a lot of stock in that rumor," said Angela Uttaro, an analyst with Gruntal & Co Inc. in New York.

KKR has been extremely active in the current boom of corporate mergers and acquisitions. And a new KKR fund which has raised nearly $5 billion has prompted widespread speculation about its future plans.

One recent connection between Kmart and KKR was the naming of James Adamson as a director in March. Adamson is chief executive of Flagstar Cos. Inc., which operates Denny's and is 47 percent owned by KKR, Uttaro said.
Adamson is among nine new board members to join Kmart since Floyd Hall was named chairman and chief executive of the discount store giant in 1995.

The overhaul was in answer to angry calls from shareholders for more outside oversight of Kmart's management. The company narrowly escaped filing for bankruptcy earlier this year before it completed a $4.7 billion new financing package in June.

The financing, which included a three-year, $3.7 billion credit facility and a $1 billion public offering of preferred securities, bought Hall and his new management team time to execute an overhaul. The financing provided an estimated $700 million in excess borrowing capacity above Kmart's peak funding needs for 1996.
"The company doesn't really need capital," said one Wall Street analyst. "They've got two or three years before they have to redo it."

Still, Kmart's shares are undervalued in light of the potential for bounceback under Hall's turnaround strategy, analysts said. The stock, which closed at about $11.125 in early October, has been on a downward path ever since Kmart sales turned sour at its discount stores this fall.
Kmart's shares closed up nearly 12 percent Tuesday, rising $1.125 to $10.75 on the New York Stock Exchange.

"People feel stock is cheap enough that there could be some credence to the rumor," said Bill Floersch, a market maker at the Chicago Board Options Exchange. "But whether it has chance of being real or not, who knows?"

On Wednesday, Kmart is expected to report earnings recovered substantially in the third quarter. Wall Street analysts estimate the company will report it broke even in the third quarter vs. a loss last year.

In the second quarter, Kmart broke a streak of 13 consecutive quarters of earnings declines or losses. The company's recovery has been aided by asset sales and cost savings, which came to $224 million in the first six months of this year. A similar level of savings is expected in the second half of the year.
KKR holds the record for the largest-ever U.S. acquisition with its 1988 purchase of RJR Nabisco for $24.6 billion.
